goals: Describe the structure of a polynucleotide and of the DNA double helix
Explain how DNA is packaged in prokaryotes and eukaryotes
Explain the experiments of Griffith, Avery and colleagues, and Hershey and Chase
Compare DNA and RNA as genetic material

slides.heading: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what Mendel’s “factors” are made of: the structure of DNA, how it is packed, and how scientists proved it is the genetic material.

visual.alt: Flow from gene to DNA sequence, RNA, protein and trait

slides.narration: In the last chapter we treated genes as abstract factors. Now we look at what they are made of. Genes are stretches of DNA, a long molecule that stores information in its sequence of bases. We will see its structure, how metres of it fit into a tiny nucleus, and the clever experiments that proved DNA is the genetic material.

slides.heading: DNA sizes
slides.body_md: DNA is a long polymer of **deoxyribonucleotides**. Its length is usually given as the number of nucleotides, or **base pairs (bp)** for double-stranded DNA.

visual.alt: Table of genome sizes of two bacteriophages, E. coli and humans

slides.narration: Genomes vary enormously in size. A small virus has a few thousand nucleotides, the bacterium E. coli has about four point six million base pairs, and a human haploid set has about three point three billion. Every one of these is copied and read by the same basic chemistry.

slides.heading: Building a polynucleotide
slides.body_md: A **nucleotide** = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate. Base + sugar (joined by an **N-glycosidic** linkage) = **nucleoside**. A phosphate on the 5′ carbon makes a nucleotide. Nucleotides join by **3′–5′ phosphodiester** linkages, giving a strand with a free **5′ phosphate** end and a free **3′ OH** end.

visual.alt: Table comparing the sugars and bases of DNA and RNA

slides.narration: Think of a necklace. Each bead is a nucleotide: a sugar with a base attached on one side and a phosphate on the other. The phosphate of one nucleotide links to the sugar of the next, forming a sugar-phosphate backbone, with the bases sticking out. One end of the chain is called five prime, the other three prime.

slides.heading: The double helix
slides.body_md: Two polynucleotide chains run **antiparallel**. Bases pair inside: **A with T** (two hydrogen bonds) and **G with C** (three). A purine always faces a pyrimidine, so the distance between the strands stays constant.

slides.narration: Here the helix is drawn untwisted, like a ladder. The rails are the sugar-phosphate backbones; the rungs are base pairs. Notice that one strand runs five prime to three prime from left to right, and the other the opposite way. Given one strand, you can always write the other, because pairing is complementary.

slides.heading: Watson and Crick’s model
slides.body_md: In **1953** Watson and Crick proposed the double helix, using **X-ray diffraction** data from **Maurice Wilkins** and **Rosalind Franklin**, and **Chargaff’s rule** that in double-stranded DNA A = T and G = C.

visual.alt: Table of the dimensions and features of the Watson–Crick double helix

slides.narration: The model fitted all the evidence. Franklin’s X-ray photographs showed a helix with regular repeats. Chargaff had found that adenine always equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine. Watson and Crick realised that complementary base pairing explains both, and also suggests how DNA could be copied.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Chargaff’s rule
slides.body_md: A double-stranded DNA sample has 20 percent adenine. Find the percentages of the other bases. How many hydrogen bonds hold together a 10 bp stretch with 4 A–T and 6 G–C pairs?
bullets: Step 1 — A = T, so T = 20 percent; A + T = 40 percent.
Step 2 — G + C = 100 − 40 = 60 percent, and G = C, so each is 30 percent.
Step 3 — Hydrogen bonds $= 4 \times 2 + 6 \times 3 = 26$.

visual.alt: Worked table: A 20, T 20, G 30, C 30 percent

slides.narration: Use the pairing rule twice. Adenine equals thymine, so both are twenty percent, making forty together. The remaining sixty percent is shared equally by guanine and cytosine, thirty each. For hydrogen bonds, count two for each A–T pair and three for each G–C pair: eight plus eighteen is twenty-six.

slides.heading: Quick check: Chargaff
slides.body_md: In a double-stranded DNA, cytosine is 18 percent. What is the percentage of adenine?
slides.narration: Quick check. Pair the bases first, then share out what is left.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how long is the DNA?
slides.body_md: The distance between adjacent base pairs is 0.34 nm. Find the length of the DNA in a human diploid cell (6.6 × 10⁹ bp) and in E. coli (4.6 × 10⁶ bp).
bullets: Step 1 — Human: $6.6 \times 10^{9} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{m} \approx 2.2\ \text{m}$.
Step 2 — E. coli: $4.6 \times 10^{6} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{m} \approx 1.56\ \text{mm}$.
Conclusion — about two metres of DNA must fit into a nucleus a few micrometres across; it must be packed very tightly.

visual.alt: Worked table: human DNA about 2.2 metres, E. coli DNA about 1.56 millimetres

slides.narration: Multiply the number of base pairs by the length of one, zero point three four nanometres. For a human diploid cell this gives about two point two metres of DNA, in a nucleus only a few micrometres wide. For E. coli it is about one point five six millimetres. Packing is clearly essential.

slides.heading: Packaging DNA
slides.body_md: In **prokaryotes**, negatively charged DNA is held in large loops by positively charged proteins in a region called the **nucleoid**. In **eukaryotes**, DNA wraps around **histones**, proteins rich in the basic amino acids **lysine and arginine**, which carry positive charges.

rows: Histones (lysine, arginine) and non-histone chromosomal proteins

visual.alt: Table comparing DNA packaging in prokaryotes and eukaryotes

slides.narration: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups. Positively charged proteins attract it and help fold it. In eukaryotes, eight histone molecules form a core called the histone octamer, and the DNA winds around it. This makes a structure called a nucleosome.

slides.heading: Nucleosomes
slides.body_md: A **nucleosome** has about **200 bp** of DNA wrapped around a **histone octamer**. Repeating nucleosomes form a **"beads-on-string"** chromatin fibre, which coils further and condenses into **chromosomes** at metaphase.

slides.narration: Under an electron microscope, chromatin looks like beads on a string. Each bead is a nucleosome, and the string is linker DNA. The fibre then coils and loops into higher-order structures with the help of non-histone proteins, condensing most at metaphase, when chromosomes are easiest to see.

slides.heading: Euchromatin and heterochromatin
slides.body_md: Chromatin is not packed uniformly in the nucleus.

visual.alt: Table comparing euchromatin and heterochromatin

slides.narration: Some regions are loosely packed and stain lightly; these are euchromatin, where genes are being read. Other regions are densely packed and stain darkly; this is heterochromatin, which is largely inactive. Packing therefore also helps control which genes are used.

slides.heading: Quick check: active chromatin
slides.body_md: Which kind of chromatin is loosely packed and transcriptionally active?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember: loose packing makes genes easier to read.

slides.heading: Griffith’s transforming principle (1928)
slides.body_md: **Frederick Griffith** worked with *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: the **S strain** (smooth, with a capsule) kills mice; the **R strain** (rough, no capsule) does not.

rows: Mice die; live S bacteria recovered

visual.alt: Table of Griffith’s four injections and their results

slides.narration: The last result was the surprise. Neither heat-killed S bacteria nor live R bacteria could kill mice on their own, but together they did, and living S bacteria appeared in the dead mice. Something from the dead S cells had transformed the harmless R cells. Griffith called it the transforming principle, but he did not know what it was.

slides.heading: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty; Hershey and Chase
slides.body_md: **Avery, MacLeod and McCarty** purified the components of heat-killed S cells: only **DNA** transformed R cells; proteases and RNase did not stop transformation, but **DNase** did. **Hershey and Chase (1952)** grew bacteriophages with radioactive **³²P** (labels DNA) or **³⁵S** (labels protein): only ³²P entered the bacteria.

nodes.label: Bacteria not radioactive: protein stayed outside

visual.alt: Flow of the Hershey–Chase experiment showing that radioactive phosphorus, not sulphur, entered bacteria

slides.narration: Avery’s group showed that destroying DNA, but not protein or RNA, stopped transformation. Hershey and Chase used a neat trick: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulphur, and protein coats contain sulphur but no phosphorus. After infection, the bacteria carried radioactive phosphorus, not sulphur. So only the DNA had entered and directed new viruses.

slides.heading: Properties of genetic material; DNA versus RNA
slides.body_md: Genetic material must **replicate**, be **chemically and structurally stable**, allow **slow changes (mutation)** for evolution, and **express** itself as characters. Both nucleic acids can direct their duplication, but DNA is better for storage.

rows: More stable: no reactive 2′ OH; thymine instead of uracil
Less stable; 2′ OH makes it reactive and easily degraded
Fast (RNA viruses mutate and evolve quickly)
Can directly code for proteins; some RNAs are catalysts
Genetic material of some viruses (for example TMV, QB bacteriophage)

visual.alt: Table comparing DNA and RNA as genetic material

slides.narration: RNA was probably the first genetic material, because it can both store information and act as a catalyst. But its extra hydroxyl group makes it reactive and less stable. DNA, with its double strands and thymine, is more stable and mutates more slowly, so it took over as the main store of genetic information, while RNA became the messenger.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate; phosphodiester linkages; 5′ and 3′ ends; purines A, G; pyrimidines C, T (DNA), U (RNA).
Double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953): antiparallel strands; A=T, G≡C; pitch 3.4 nm; about 10 bp per turn; 0.34 nm per bp.
Packaging: nucleoid in prokaryotes; nucleosomes (about 200 bp around a histone octamer) in eukaryotes; euchromatin active, heterochromatin inactive.
Griffith: transformation; Avery, MacLeod, McCarty: DNA transforms; Hershey–Chase: ³²P (DNA) enters bacteria.
DNA is more stable than RNA; RNA was probably the first genetic material.

rows: DNA, not protein, enters and directs the cell

visual.alt: Summary table of three experiments and their conclusions

slides.narration: To recap: DNA is a double helix of antiparallel strands held by complementary base pairs. Metres of it are packed into nucleosomes and chromatin. A chain of experiments, from Griffith to Hershey and Chase, proved that DNA is the genetic material, and its stability makes it better suited than RNA for storing information.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Use Chargaff: **A = T, G = C** only for **double-stranded** DNA.
Give the **double-helix numbers** exactly: 3.4 nm, 10 bp, 0.34 nm.
For Hershey–Chase, explain **why** ³²P and ³⁵S label DNA and protein.
Write **euchromatin = active**, **heterochromatin = inactive**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Apply Chargaff’s rule only to double-stranded DNA. Learn the helix dimensions. In the Hershey and Chase experiment, explain why phosphorus labels DNA and sulphur labels protein. And remember which chromatin is active.

slides.heading: From DNA to protein
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how DNA is copied, how its message is transcribed into RNA, and how RNA is translated into protein.

visual.alt: Flow of the central dogma: DNA replicates, is transcribed into RNA and translated into protein

slides.narration: The central dogma, proposed by Francis Crick, says that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. DNA copies itself in replication, its message is copied into RNA in transcription, and the RNA message is decoded into protein in translation. In some viruses, information flows from RNA back to DNA, called reverse transcription.

slides.heading: Semi-conservative replication
slides.body_md: Watson and Crick proposed that the two strands **separate** and each acts as a **template** for a new complementary strand. Each daughter molecule then has **one parental and one new strand**: **semi-conservative** replication.

nodes.label: Two daughter molecules: one old + one new strand each

visual.alt: Flow of semi-conservative replication from parent helix to two daughters each with one old and one new strand

slides.narration: Complementary pairing suggests a simple copying method. Unzip the two strands, and use each as a guide to build a new partner. The two daughter molecules are identical to the parent, and each keeps one of the original strands. That is what semi-conservative means: half conserved, half new.

slides.heading: The Meselson–Stahl experiment (1958)
slides.body_md: E. coli was grown for many generations in **¹⁵NH₄Cl** (heavy nitrogen), then transferred to normal **¹⁴N** medium. DNA was separated by density in a **caesium chloride (CsCl) gradient**.

After two generations there were equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA. Exactly as semi-conservative replication predicts.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: predicting the bands
slides.body_md: Using semi-conservative replication, predict the fractions of hybrid and light DNA after 1, 2, 3 and 4 generations in ¹⁴N medium.
bullets: Rule — the two original heavy strands always end up in exactly 2 molecules; after $n$ generations there are $2^n$ molecules.
So hybrid fraction $= \dfrac{2}{2^n}$, and light fraction $= 1 - \dfrac{2}{2^n}$.
Generation 1: hybrid 100 percent, light 0 percent.
Generation 2: hybrid 50 percent, light 50 percent.
Generation 3: hybrid 25 percent, light 75 percent.
Generation 4: hybrid 12.5 percent, light 87.5 percent.

visual.alt: Worked table of hybrid and light DNA percentages after one to four generations

slides.narration: The two heavy strands from the start are never destroyed; each sits in a separate molecule paired with a light strand. After n generations there are two to the power n molecules, but still only two hybrids. So after three generations a quarter is hybrid, and after four, one eighth.

slides.body_md: After two generations in ¹⁴N medium, what does semi-conservative replication predict?
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the rule: two hybrids among all the molecules.

slides.body_md: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the **5′ → 3′** direction. At a **replication fork**, one strand (**leading**) is made **continuously**; the other (**lagging**) is made **discontinuously** as **Okazaki fragments**, later joined by **DNA ligase**.

The lagging strand is made in short pieces, called Okazaki fragments, each starting near the fork and growing away from it. DNA ligase seals the pieces into one strand.

slides.heading: The replication machinery
slides.body_md: Replication needs a set of enzymes and energy, and starts at definite points.

rows: Main enzyme; very fast and accurate (E. coli copies 4.6 × 10⁶ bp in about 18 minutes, roughly 2000 bp per second)
Act as substrates and provide energy for polymerisation
Definite region where replication starts; a plasmid or vector needs one to be copied
In eukaryotes, during the S phase of the cell cycle

visual.alt: Table of requirements for DNA replication and their roles

slides.narration: DNA polymerase works astonishingly fast and makes very few mistakes. The building blocks, deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates, do double duty: they are both the raw material and the energy source. Replication starts at specific origins, which is why any DNA we want a cell to copy must carry one.

slides.heading: Transcription
slides.body_md: A **transcription unit** has a **promoter**, a **structural gene** and a **terminator**. Only **one strand**, the **template strand** (3′ → 5′), is copied; the other, the **coding strand** (5′ → 3′), has the same sequence as the RNA except **T in place of U**.

slides.narration: If both strands were transcribed, the two RNAs would be complementary and would stick together, and one gene would code for two different proteins. So only one strand is read. The promoter, upstream, is where RNA polymerase binds; the terminator, downstream, is where transcription stops. By convention, sequences are written using the coding strand.

slides.heading: Transcription in bacteria and in eukaryotes
slides.body_md: Bacteria have **one RNA polymerase**; eukaryotes have **three** in the nucleus, and their primary transcripts are processed.

rows: One; σ factor for initiation, ρ factor for termination
I: rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); II: hnRNA, the precursor of mRNA; III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs
None needed; translation can begin before transcription ends
Splicing removes introns and joins exons; capping adds methyl guanosine triphosphate at 5′; tailing adds 200–300 adenylates at 3′

visual.alt: Table comparing transcription in bacteria and eukaryotes

slides.narration: Eukaryotic genes are split: coding exons are interrupted by non-coding introns. The first transcript, heterogeneous nuclear RNA, contains both. Splicing cuts out the introns and joins the exons. A cap is added at the five prime end and a poly-A tail at the three prime end. Only then is the mature messenger RNA sent out to the cytoplasm.

slides.heading: Quick check: RNA polymerase II
slides.body_md: In eukaryotes, which RNA polymerase transcribes the precursor of mRNA?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the job of each of the three polymerases.

slides.heading: The genetic code
slides.body_md: George Gamow argued that with 4 bases and 20 amino acids, the code should be a **triplet** (4³ = 64 combinations). Har Gobind **Khorana** made RNAs of known sequence, and Marshall **Nirenberg** used a cell-free system to decode them.

rows: 64 codons: 61 code for amino acids, 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA)
One codon codes for only one amino acid
Some amino acids have more than one codon
Same from bacteria to humans, with a few exceptions
Codes for methionine and acts as the start codon

visual.alt: Table of features of the genetic code

slides.narration: A doublet code would give only sixteen words, too few for twenty amino acids, so the code must use triplets, giving sixty-four. Sixty-one codons specify amino acids and three mean stop. The code is read without commas, each codon means only one amino acid, many amino acids have several codons, and the same code is used almost everywhere in life.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from template to protein
slides.body_md: A template strand reads 3′–TACAAACCGTTTATC–5′. Write the mRNA and the amino acid sequence it codes for.
bullets: Step 1 — mRNA is complementary to the template, with U for T: 5′–AUGUUUGGCAAAUAG–3′.
Step 2 — Read codons from AUG: AUG UUU GGC AAA UAG.
Step 3 — Translate: Met–Phe–Gly–Lys, then the stop codon ends the chain.

visual.alt: Worked table: codons AUG, UUU, GGC, AAA, UAG give Met, Phe, Gly, Lys and stop

slides.narration: First write the messenger RNA, pairing each template base with its partner and using U instead of T. Then split the message into triplets, starting at the start codon, and look up each codon. The final triplet is a stop codon, so translation ends there. The result is a short chain of four amino acids beginning with methionine.

slides.heading: Mutations and the reading frame
slides.body_md: Because codons are read contiguously, the effect of a mutation depends on how many bases change.

rows: Changes one codon; may change one amino acid (sickle-cell: GAG → GUG, Glu → Val)
Insertion or deletion of one or two bases
Frameshift: every codon after the change is misread
Insertion or deletion of three bases
One amino acid added or removed; the frame after it is restored

visual.alt: Table of the effects of substitution, frameshift and three-base mutations

slides.narration: Think of a sentence made of three-letter words. Change one letter, and one word changes. Add or remove one letter, and every word after it becomes nonsense; that is a frameshift. Add or remove three letters, and you gain or lose one word, but the rest still reads correctly. Experiments like this confirmed that the code is a triplet read without gaps.

slides.heading: tRNA, the adapter
slides.body_md: **tRNA** links codons to amino acids. It has an **anticodon** loop that pairs with a codon and an **amino acid acceptor end**. Its secondary structure looks like a **clover leaf**; in three dimensions, an **inverted L**.

rows: A specific tRNA for each amino acid
A special tRNA carries methionine to start translation
Amino acids are activated with ATP and linked to their tRNA (aminoacylation)

visual.alt: Table of features of tRNA

slides.narration: An amino acid cannot recognise a codon by itself, so tRNA acts as an adapter. One end carries a specific amino acid; the other end has an anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA. There is no tRNA for the stop codons, which is why they end translation.

slides.heading: Translation
slides.body_md: Translation is the polymerisation of amino acids into a polypeptide, in the order set by the mRNA codons, on **ribosomes**.

nodes.label: Initiation: small ribosome subunit meets mRNA; start codon AUG; large subunit joins
Elongation: charged tRNAs bind codon by codon; peptide bonds form
Termination: a release factor binds the stop codon; polypeptide released

visual.alt: Flow of translation: charging, initiation at AUG, elongation and termination at a stop codon

slides.narration: The ribosome has two subunits that come together on the messenger RNA at the start codon. Charged tRNAs arrive one by one, pairing with each codon, and the ribosome links their amino acids with peptide bonds. In bacteria, a ribosomal RNA, the twenty-three S rRNA, catalyses this bond, so it is a ribozyme. At a stop codon, a release factor frees the finished chain. Untranslated regions at each end help translation work efficiently.

slides.heading: Quick check: a ribozyme
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the ribosome.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which molecule in the ribosome forms peptide bonds in bacteria?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Replication is semi-conservative (Meselson and Stahl, ¹⁵N/¹⁴N, CsCl gradient); DNA polymerase works 5′ → 3′; leading strand continuous, lagging strand as Okazaki fragments joined by ligase.
Transcription unit: promoter, structural gene, terminator; template 3′ → 5′; RNA made 5′ → 3′.
Bacteria: one RNA polymerase (σ, ρ). Eukaryotes: pol I (rRNAs), II (hnRNA), III (tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNA); splicing, capping, tailing.
Code: triplet, 61 sense + 3 stop codons, unambiguous, degenerate, contiguous, nearly universal; AUG = Met and start.
Translation: charging, initiation, elongation (23S rRNA is a ribozyme in bacteria), termination by a release factor.

visual.alt: Summary table of replication, transcription and translation

slides.narration: To recap: DNA copies itself semi-conservatively, with leading and lagging strands. Genes are transcribed from one strand into RNA, which in eukaryotes is spliced, capped and tailed. The triplet code is read by tRNAs on ribosomes to build proteins, from a start codon to a stop codon.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: When writing mRNA from DNA, check **which strand** you are given; mRNA matches the **coding** strand (U for T).
Explain **why** the lagging strand is discontinuous: polymerase works only **5′ → 3′**.
List the **three eukaryotic RNA polymerases** with products.
Give **features of the code** with examples (UAA, UAG, UGA; AUG).
slides.narration: Exam tips. Always check whether a question gives the template or the coding strand. Explain the lagging strand using the five prime to three prime rule. Learn the three RNA polymerases. And quote the stop codons and the start codon when describing the genetic code.

slides.heading: Regulation, genomes and fingerprints
slides.body_md: Part 3 — how cells switch genes on and off, what we learned by reading the whole human genome, and how DNA can identify a person.

visual.alt: Flow of topics in Part 3

slides.narration: Every cell carries the full set of genes, yet a cell does not use them all at once. In this part we see how a bacterium switches a set of genes on only when it needs them. Then we look at the huge project that read the human genome, and at DNA fingerprinting, which uses differences in our DNA to identify individuals.

slides.heading: Levels of gene regulation
slides.body_md: Gene expression can be regulated at several levels in eukaryotes; in **prokaryotes**, control is mainly at the **initiation of transcription**.

rows: Whether the primary transcript is made
Movement of mRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm
Whether and how fast the mRNA is translated

visual.alt: Table of four levels of regulation of gene expression

slides.narration: A cell can control a gene at many points: making the RNA, processing it, moving it out of the nucleus, or translating it. Bacteria mostly decide at the very first step: whether RNA polymerase is allowed to start transcribing. The best-known example is the lac operon of E. coli, which handles the sugar lactose.

slides.heading: The lac operon
slides.body_md: An **operon** is a set of genes controlled together. The **lac operon** (Jacob and Monod) has a regulatory gene **i**, a **promoter**, an **operator** and three structural genes: **z** (β-galactosidase), **y** (permease) and **a** (transacetylase).

slides.narration: The regulatory gene i makes a repressor protein all the time. With no lactose, the repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase, so the structural genes stay silent. When lactose is present, it acts as the inducer: it binds the repressor and changes its shape so it falls off the operator, and transcription begins.

slides.heading: How the switch works
slides.body_md: The lac operon is under **negative regulation**: the repressor switches it **off**; the **inducer** (lactose) switches it **on** by inactivating the repressor.

nodes.label: RNA polymerase blocked: no enzymes made
Inducer binds repressor; repressor leaves operator
z, y, a transcribed: enzymes break down lactose
Lactose used up: repressor binds again

visual.alt: Flow of lac operon regulation from off to on and back to off

slides.narration: This is an elegant economy. The cell makes the lactose-digesting enzymes only when lactose is present. A small amount of permease lets some lactose in, which switches the operon on. When all the lactose has been broken down, the repressor is free again, binds the operator and switches the genes off.

slides.body_md: What switches on the lac operon?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which molecule removes the repressor from the operator?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: predicting mutants
slides.body_md: Predict whether β-galactosidase is made, with and without lactose, in three mutant bacteria.
bullets: Mutant 1 — the **i gene** makes a non-functional repressor: nothing blocks the operator, so enzymes are made **all the time** (with or without lactose).
Mutant 2 — the **operator** is changed so the repressor cannot bind: again **always on**.
Mutant 3 — the **z gene** is non-functional: the operon can be switched on, but **no active β-galactosidase** is ever made.

visual.alt: Worked table of β-galactosidase production in normal and three mutant bacteria with and without lactose

slides.narration: Trace what each part does. Without a working repressor, or without an operator it can bind to, nothing can switch the operon off, so the enzymes are made constantly. If the structural gene for beta-galactosidase is broken, switching the operon on does not help, because the enzyme itself cannot be made correctly.

slides.heading: The Human Genome Project
slides.body_md: The **Human Genome Project (HGP)** was launched in **1990** and completed in **2003**, a huge project in which many countries took part.

rows: About 20 000 to 25 000 genes in human DNA
To other sectors, such as industry
Address ethical, legal and social issues

visual.alt: Table of the goals of the Human Genome Project

slides.narration: The project aimed to read every base of human DNA and find every gene. That needed new machines, new computer methods and huge databases. Its organisers also set aside effort to study the ethical, legal and social questions, because genetic information is personal and powerful.

slides.heading: How the genome was read
slides.body_md: Two approaches were used: identifying all genes expressed as RNA (**Expressed Sequence Tags, ESTs**) and **sequence annotation** (sequencing everything, then assigning functions).

nodes.label: Cloned in hosts using BAC and YAC vectors

visual.alt: Flow of genome sequencing: fragmenting DNA, cloning in BAC and YAC vectors, automated sequencing and computer alignment

slides.narration: The genome is far too long to sequence in one piece. It was broken into small fragments, which were copied in bacteria or yeast using special vectors called bacterial and yeast artificial chromosomes. Each piece was sequenced with automated machines based on Frederick Sanger’s method, and computers found the overlaps to assemble the whole sequence.

slides.heading: What the genome showed
slides.body_md: Some salient observations of the HGP:

rows: About 3000 bases; the largest, dystrophin, 2.4 million bases
Less than 2 percent of the genome

visual.alt: Table of salient findings of the Human Genome Project

slides.narration: Some findings were surprising. Less than two percent of our DNA codes for proteins; much of the rest is made of repeated sequences. Any two people share about ninety-nine point nine percent of their DNA bases. The functions of over half the discovered genes were still unknown when the project ended.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: putting the numbers to work
slides.body_md: The human genome has 3164.7 million bases. About how many bases code for proteins if the coding share is 2 percent? If two people differ at 0.1 percent of bases, at about how many positions do they differ?
bullets: Step 1 — Coding bases $\approx 3164.7 \times 10^{6} \times 0.02 \approx 63.3$ million (an upper estimate, since less than 2 percent codes).
Step 2 — Differences $\approx 3164.7 \times 10^{6} \times 0.001 \approx 3.16$ million positions.
Conclusion — even 0.1 percent means millions of differences, which is what makes every person’s DNA unique.

visual.alt: Worked table of coding bases and differences between two people

slides.narration: Multiply the total by each fraction. Two percent of about three thousand one hundred and sixty-five million is about sixty-three million bases, at most. And one tenth of one percent is about three point two million positions. So even though we are almost identical, there are millions of differences between any two people, the basis of DNA fingerprinting.

slides.heading: Quick check: genome facts
slides.body_md: Which chromosome was found to carry the most genes?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the chromosomes with the most and the fewest genes.

slides.heading: The basis of DNA fingerprinting
slides.body_md: DNA fingerprinting compares **repetitive DNA**, short sequences repeated many times. In density-gradient centrifugation these form small peaks of **satellite DNA**. Some of them, **VNTRs** (variable number tandem repeats), differ in repeat number between people: **polymorphism**.

rows: Small stretches of DNA repeated many times
Repetitive DNA forming minor peaks in a density gradient; does not code for proteins
A satellite sequence whose copy number varies between individuals; fragment sizes from about 0.1 to 20 kb
Variation at a DNA sequence between individuals, inherited from parents

visual.alt: Table of terms used in DNA fingerprinting

slides.narration: Our DNA contains many short sequences repeated over and over. The number of repeats at certain places, called variable number tandem repeats, differs from person to person. So the sizes of these pieces form a pattern unique to each individual, except identical twins. Half of each person’s pattern comes from each parent.

slides.heading: Steps of DNA fingerprinting
slides.body_md: The technique was developed by **Alec Jeffreys**, using a VNTR as a probe.

nodes.label: Transfer to a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane (Southern blotting)
Hybridise with a labelled VNTR probe
Detect by autoradiography: pattern of bands

visual.alt: Flow of the steps of DNA fingerprinting

slides.narration: First the DNA is extracted and cut with restriction enzymes. The fragments are separated by size in a gel, then blotted onto a membrane. A labelled VNTR probe sticks only to matching fragments, and an X-ray film reveals them as a pattern of bands. Tiny samples, such as a drop of blood or a hair root, can be used.

slides.heading: Reading a fingerprint
slides.body_md: A child’s bands must each match a band of the **mother** or of the **biological father**. Uses: **forensic** identification, **paternity** disputes, and studies of **population and genetic diversity**.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Prokaryotic regulation mainly at initiation of transcription; lac operon: i (repressor), p, o, z (β-galactosidase), y (permease), a (transacetylase); lactose is the inducer; negative regulation.
HGP (1990–2003): goals, ESTs and sequence annotation, BAC and YAC vectors, automated Sanger sequencing.
Findings: 3164.7 million bases; about 30 000 genes; 99.9 percent identical; under 2 percent coding; chromosome 1 most genes, Y fewest; 1.4 million SNPs.
DNA fingerprinting (Jeffreys): VNTRs, polymorphism; isolate → digest → electrophoresis → blot → hybridise → autoradiograph; forensic and paternity uses.

visual.alt: Summary table of key words for the three topics

slides.narration: To recap: the lac operon is switched on only when lactose inactivates the repressor. The Human Genome Project read over three billion bases and found that very little of our DNA codes for proteins. And DNA fingerprinting uses variable repeats to give each person a unique pattern of bands, half from each parent.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name all parts of the lac operon with the **product of each structural gene**.
Call lac operon control **negative regulation** and name **lactose as the inducer**.
List the **steps of DNA fingerprinting in order** — a favourite 3- or 5-mark question.
Quote HGP numbers carefully: **3164.7 million bases**, **under 2 percent coding**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the parts of the lac operon and what each structural gene makes. Describe the control as negative regulation with lactose as the inducer. Practise the steps of DNA fingerprinting in the right order. And quote the genome project numbers precisely.

notes.title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The search for the genetic material
sections.body_md:
**Griffith (1928),** *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: S strain (capsule, virulent) and R strain (no capsule). Live S → mice die; live R → live; heat-killed S → live; heat-killed S + live R → mice die and live S recovered. Some "transforming principle" from dead S cells **transformed** R cells.

**Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933–44):** purified DNA, RNA and proteins from heat-killed S cells; only **DNA** transformed R cells. Proteases and RNase did not stop transformation; **DNase** did.

**Hershey and Chase (1952):** bacteriophages grown with radioactive **³²P** (DNA contains P, protein does not) or **³⁵S** (protein contains S, DNA does not). After infection, blending and centrifugation, bacteria infected with ³²P phages were radioactive, those with ³⁵S phages were not: **DNA enters the bacterium and is the genetic material**.

**Criteria for genetic material:** replicates; chemically and structurally stable; allows slow changes (mutation) for evolution; expresses itself as Mendelian characters. **DNA vs RNA:** RNA's 2′-OH makes it reactive and less stable, and it mutates faster; uracil in RNA is replaced by the more stable thymine in DNA. RNA was probably the first genetic material ("RNA world"); some viruses (TMV, QB bacteriophage) still use RNA.

key_terms.definition_md: Change in the genetic make-up of a bacterium caused by DNA taken up from another strain.

nodes.label: Avery et al.: it is DNA

visual.alt: Flow of experiments proving DNA is the genetic material

sections.heading: 2. Structure of DNA and RNA; packaging
sections.body_md:
**Polynucleotide:** nitrogenous base + pentose (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) + phosphate. Base + sugar (N-glycosidic linkage) = nucleoside; + phosphate (phosphoester at 5′-OH) = nucleotide; nucleotides joined by **3′–5′ phosphodiester** linkages. Purines: adenine, guanine; pyrimidines: cytosine, thymine (DNA), uracil (RNA). DNA was first identified by Friedrich Miescher (1869) as "nuclein".

**Double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953;** X-ray data of Wilkins and Franklin; **Chargaff**: A = T, G = C in double-stranded DNA):
- two **antiparallel** polynucleotide chains, sugar-phosphate backbone outside, bases inside;
- **A=T (two H-bonds)**, **G≡C (three H-bonds)**; a purine always faces a pyrimidine (uniform width);
- right-handed; pitch **3.4 nm**; about **10 bp per turn**; **0.34 nm** between base pairs.
Length = number of bp × 0.34 nm: human diploid DNA (6.6 × 10⁹ bp) ≈ 2.2 m; E. coli (4.6 × 10⁶ bp) ≈ 1.56 mm.

**Packaging:** prokaryotes — DNA in large loops held by positively charged proteins in the **nucleoid**. Eukaryotes — **histones** (rich in lysine and arginine; positive) form an **octamer**; DNA wraps around it as a **nucleosome** (about 200 bp); nucleosomes form the "beads-on-string" chromatin fibre, which coils further; **non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins** help higher packing. **Euchromatin:** loosely packed, light-staining, transcriptionally active. **Heterochromatin:** densely packed, dark-staining, inactive.

key_terms.definition_md: Unit of chromatin: about 200 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.
Running in opposite directions: one strand 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′.

sections.heading: 3. DNA replication
sections.body_md:
**Semi-conservative** (Watson and Crick): strands separate and each templates a new strand, so each daughter has one old and one new strand.

**Meselson and Stahl (1958):** E. coli grown in **¹⁵NH₄Cl**, then in ¹⁴N; DNA separated in a **CsCl density gradient**. Generation 1: all hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N); generation 2: hybrid and light in equal amounts. After *n* generations, hybrid fraction = 2/2ⁿ. (Taylor and colleagues showed the same in *Vicia faba* chromosomes using radioactive thymidine.)

**Machinery:** DNA-dependent **DNA polymerase** (polymerises only **5′ → 3′**; E. coli copies 4.6 × 10⁶ bp in about 18 minutes, roughly 2000 bp/s); deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates are substrates and energy source; replication starts at an **origin of replication**; at the **replication fork** the **leading strand** is continuous and the **lagging strand** is made as **Okazaki fragments** joined by **DNA ligase**. In eukaryotes replication occurs in the **S phase**.

key_terms.definition_md: Each new DNA molecule has one parental and one newly made strand.

sections.heading: 4. Transcription and the genetic code
sections.body_md:
**Central dogma** (Crick): DNA → RNA → protein; **reverse transcription** (RNA → DNA) in some viruses (retroviruses).

**Transcription unit:** **promoter** (upstream, binding site of RNA polymerase), **structural gene**, **terminator**. Template strand 3′→5′; coding strand 5′→3′ has the RNA sequence (T for U). Structural genes may be monocistronic (mostly eukaryotes) or polycistronic (mostly bacteria).
- **Bacteria:** one DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; **σ** (initiation) and **ρ** (termination) factors; transcription and translation can be coupled.
- **Eukaryotes:** **RNA pol I** (rRNAs 28S, 18S, 5.8S), **pol II** (hnRNA → mRNA), **pol III** (tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs). **Split genes**: exons (coding) and introns. Processing: **splicing** (remove introns, join exons), **capping** (methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5′ end), **tailing** (200–300 adenylates at the 3′ end).

**Genetic code:** proposed as a triplet by Gamow (4³ = 64); RNAs of defined sequence made by **Khorana**; cell-free decoding by **Nirenberg**. Features: triplet; 61 sense codons, 3 stop (UAA, UAG, UGA); unambiguous and specific; degenerate; read contiguously (no punctuation); nearly universal; **AUG** codes for methionine and is the start codon. **Mutations:** a point mutation changes one codon (sickle-cell GAG → GUG); insertion or deletion of 1–2 bases causes a **frameshift**; of 3 bases adds or removes one amino acid.

key_terms.definition_md: DNA sequence upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription.
Coding sequences retained in mature mRNA / intervening sequences removed by splicing.
Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon.

sections.heading: 5. tRNA and translation
sections.body_md:
**tRNA (adapter):** clover-leaf secondary structure, inverted-L 3D shape; **anticodon loop** pairs with the codon; **amino acid acceptor end** carries the amino acid; a specific tRNA for each amino acid; an **initiator tRNA** for methionine; **no tRNA for stop codons**.

**Translation:**
1. **Charging (aminoacylation):** amino acids activated with ATP and linked to their tRNA.
2. **Initiation:** the small ribosomal subunit meets the mRNA at the start codon **AUG**; the large subunit joins.
3. **Elongation:** charged tRNAs enter codon by codon; peptide bonds form. In bacteria the **23S rRNA** catalyses peptide-bond formation, acting as a **ribozyme**.
4. **Termination:** a **release factor** binds the stop codon; the polypeptide is released.

**UTRs** (untranslated regions) at the 5′ and 3′ ends of mRNA help efficient translation.

key_terms.definition_md: Three bases of tRNA that pair with a codon on mRNA.
An RNA that acts as an enzyme, such as 23S rRNA in bacterial ribosomes.

sections.heading: 6. Regulation of gene expression: the lac operon
sections.body_md:
Regulation can occur at transcription, processing, transport of mRNA or translation; in prokaryotes it is mainly at the **initiation of transcription**. An **operon** is a set of genes controlled together.

**lac operon (Jacob and Monod):** regulatory gene **i** (makes the **repressor**), **promoter**, **operator**, structural genes **z** (β-galactosidase: lactose → galactose + glucose), **y** (permease: lets lactose in), **a** (transacetylase).
- **No lactose:** the repressor binds the **operator** and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.
- **Lactose present (inducer):** lactose binds the repressor, inactivating it; RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a.
- When lactose is used up, the repressor binds again. This is **negative regulation**.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of genes with related functions controlled together by one promoter and operator.
A substance (lactose for the lac operon) that inactivates the repressor and switches the operon on.

sections.heading: 7. Human Genome Project and DNA fingerprinting
sections.body_md:
**HGP (1990–2003).** Goals: identify all the approximately 20,000–25,000 human genes; determine the sequence of about 3 billion base pairs; store the information in databases; improve analysis tools; transfer technologies; address ethical, legal and social issues. Methods: **Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)** and **sequence annotation**; DNA fragments cloned in **BAC** and **YAC** vectors; **automated sequencers** based on **Sanger's** method; computer alignment of overlaps.

**Salient observations:** 3164.7 million bases; average gene about 3000 bases (largest, dystrophin, 2.4 million); about 30,000 genes; 99.9 % of bases identical in all people; functions of over half the genes unknown; **less than 2 %** of the genome codes for proteins; repeated sequences make up a large part; chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), Y fewest (231); about 1.4 million single-base differences (**SNPs**).

**DNA fingerprinting (Alec Jeffreys):** compares **repetitive DNA**; **satellite DNA** forms minor peaks in density gradients; **VNTRs** (variable number tandem repeats, about 0.1–20 kb) vary between individuals (**polymorphism**) and are inherited, half from each parent. Steps: isolate DNA → digest with **restriction endonucleases** → separate by **gel electrophoresis** → **Southern blot** onto nylon or nitrocellulose → **hybridise** with a labelled VNTR probe → detect by **autoradiography**. Uses: forensic identification, paternity testing, population and genetic diversity studies.

key_terms.definition_md: Variable number tandem repeat: a short sequence repeated a variable number of times, used as a probe in DNA fingerprinting.
Single nucleotide polymorphism: a single-base difference between individuals.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Applying A = T, G = C to single-stranded nucleic acids.
- Writing mRNA complementary to the coding strand (it matches the coding strand, with U for T).
- Saying DNA polymerase works 3′ → 5′, or that both new strands are continuous.
- Mixing up RNA polymerases I, II and III.
- Calling the lac operon positive regulation, or naming glucose as the inducer.
- Listing DNA fingerprinting steps out of order.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: base percentages, codon or amino acid, term, enzyme, number.
- 2–3-mark answers: experiment and conclusion; strand and direction; two or three features with explanation.
- 5-mark answers: a labelled diagram (fork, transcription unit, lac operon) with the process, or an experiment with set-up, results and conclusion.
- Case-based items: reading band patterns, a DNA or mRNA sequence, or an operon mutant.

questions.stem_md: An extract of heat-killed S-strain pneumococci is treated with DNase and then mixed with live R-strain bacteria before injection into mice. What is the most likely result?

options.text_md: The mice survive, because the DNA that transforms R cells has been destroyed.
The mice die, because the S-strain proteins are still present.
The mice die, because DNase converts R cells into S cells.
The mice survive, because DNase kills the live R bacteria.

questions.solution_md: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty found that only DNase stopped transformation: without intact DNA, R cells are not transformed, so the mice survive — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Griffith identified DNA as the transforming principle in his experiments with pneumococci.
questions.solution_md: False. Griffith showed that a transforming principle existed; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty later identified it as DNA.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the Hershey–Chase experiment, bacteria infected with phages grown in radioactive phosphorus became radioactive.

**Reason (R):** Phosphorus is present in DNA but not in protein, and only the phage DNA entered the bacteria.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: ³²P labels DNA, which is the part that enters the bacterium — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, phages labelled with ³⁵S infected bacteria; the culture was then blended and centrifuged. Where was most of the radioactivity found, and why?

options.text_md: In the bacterial pellet, because protein entered the bacteria
In the supernatant, because the labelled protein coats stayed outside the bacteria
In the bacterial pellet, because sulphur is part of DNA
Nowhere, because ³⁵S is lost during blending

questions.solution_md: Sulphur labels protein. The protein coats were removed by blending and stayed in the lighter supernatant, while the bacteria (pellet) were not radioactive — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why DNA is a better genetic material than RNA for most organisms.

answer.model_answer_md: DNA is **chemically more stable**: RNA has a reactive **2′-OH** group on every nucleotide, which makes it easily degraded, and DNA uses **thymine** instead of uracil. RNA also **mutates faster**, while genetic material should change only slowly; the double-stranded DNA helix with complementary strands is better at storing information.

questions.solution_md: Stability (2′-OH, thymine) and slower mutation.

questions.stem_md: Describe Griffith’s experiment with pneumococci and state what it showed.

answer.model_answer_md: Griffith used **S-strain** (smooth, capsulated, virulent) and **R-strain** (rough, non-virulent) *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. Live S killed mice; live R did not; **heat-killed S** did not. But **heat-killed S mixed with live R killed the mice**, and **live S bacteria** were recovered from them. He concluded that some **transforming principle** from the dead S cells had changed R cells into S cells; its chemical nature was not known.

questions.solution_md: Four injections; transformation.

marking_scheme.step: S and R strains with their effects
Heat-killed S + live R killed mice; live S recovered

questions.stem_md: Describe the experiments of Avery, MacLeod and McCarty and of Hershey and Chase, and explain how together they established that DNA is the genetic material.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Background.** Griffith had shown that heat-killed S-strain pneumococci could transform live R-strain bacteria into virulent S bacteria, through an unknown transforming principle.

**Avery, MacLeod and McCarty.** They purified DNA, RNA and proteins from heat-killed S cells and tested each for its ability to transform R cells. Only DNA transformed them. Protease and RNase did not prevent transformation, but DNase did. So the transforming principle was DNA.

**Hershey and Chase.** They grew bacteriophages in medium with radioactive phosphorus (which labels DNA) or radioactive sulphur (which labels protein). The labelled phages infected bacteria, which were then blended to remove the viral coats and centrifuged. Bacteria infected with ³²P phages were radioactive; those infected with ³⁵S phages were not. So only DNA entered the bacteria and directed the making of new viruses.

**Conclusion.** One experiment identified DNA chemically as the transforming agent; the other showed that DNA, not protein, is the material passed into cells to direct heredity.

questions.solution_md: Avery (enzymes); Hershey–Chase (isotopes); combined conclusion.

marking_scheme.step: Avery’s purification and transformation by DNA only
Hershey–Chase labelling with ³²P and ³⁵S

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** RNA viruses mutate and evolve faster than DNA-based organisms.

**Reason (R):** Some RNA molecules can act as biological catalysts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but RNA’s catalytic ability does not explain fast mutation; that is due to RNA’s instability and reactivity — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a double-stranded DNA, cytosine makes up 18 percent of the bases. What percentage is adenine?
questions.solution_md: C = G = 18 percent, so G + C = 36 percent; A + T = 64 percent, and A = T = 32 percent — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 35 percent guanine. What percentage of its bases is adenine?
A 12 bp stretch of DNA has 5 A–T pairs and 7 G–C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
questions.solution_md: A–T has 2 and G–C has 3 hydrogen bonds: $5 \times 2 + 7 \times 3 = 10 + 21 = 31$.

questions.stem_md: A plasmid has 20 000 base pairs. Taking 0.34 nm between adjacent base pairs, what is its length in micrometres?
A human diploid cell has about 6.6 × 10⁹ bp of DNA. If each nucleosome holds about 200 bp, about how many nucleosomes are there? Give your answer in millions.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{9}}{200} = 3.3 \times 10^{7}$, and $3.3 \times 10^{7} \div 10^{6} = 33$, so about 33 million.

questions.stem_md: Which kind of chromatin is loosely packed and transcriptionally active?
questions.solution_md: Euchromatin is loosely packed, stains lightly and is transcriptionally active — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Histones carry a positive charge because they are rich in

options.text_md: the acidic amino acids aspartate and glutamate
the basic amino acids lysine and arginine

questions.solution_md: Lysine and arginine have positively charged side chains, which attract the negatively charged DNA — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the DNA double helix, one strand runs 5′ → 3′ and the other 3′ → 5′; the strands are therefore said to be ______.
questions.solution_md: Antiparallel.

questions.stem_md: Match each structure (column I) with its role (column II).

Joins a base to its sugar

questions.solution_md: Phosphodiester → backbone links; N-glycosidic → base–sugar; hydrogen bonds → base pairs; histone octamer → nucleosome core.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The distance between the two sugar-phosphate backbones of DNA is the same all along the helix.

**Reason (R):** A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; a two-ring purine always faces a one-ring pyrimidine, so every base pair has the same width — option (a).

questions.stem_md: List the main features of the Watson–Crick double-helix model of DNA.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Two **polynucleotide chains** run **antiparallel**, with the sugar-phosphate backbone outside and bases inside.

2. Bases pair **complementarily**: **A with T** by two hydrogen bonds and **G with C** by three; a purine always faces a pyrimidine.

3. The chains coil as a **right-handed helix** with a **pitch of 3.4 nm**, about **10 bp per turn**, **0.34 nm** between base pairs; base pairs stack on one another, adding stability.

questions.solution_md: Antiparallel chains; complementary pairing; helix dimensions.

questions.stem_md: A human diploid cell contains about 2.2 m of DNA in a nucleus a few micrometres across. Explain how eukaryotic cells package this DNA.

answer.model_answer_md: The negatively charged DNA wraps around a positively charged **histone octamer** (histones are rich in lysine and arginine), forming **nucleosomes** of about 200 bp. Nucleosomes form a **beads-on-string** chromatin fibre, which is coiled and looped further with **non-histone proteins**, condensing most into **chromosomes** at metaphase.

questions.solution_md: Histone octamer → nucleosome → fibre → higher coils.

marking_scheme.step: Further coiling to chromatin fibres and chromosomes

questions.stem_md: After two generations in ¹⁴N medium, what does semi-conservative replication predict for E. coli DNA that started fully heavy?

options.text_md: Half hybrid and half light DNA
Half heavy and half light DNA

questions.solution_md: Hybrid fraction after n generations = 2/2ⁿ; for n = 2 this is 1/2, and the rest is light — option (b).

questions.stem_md: E. coli with fully heavy (¹⁵N) DNA is grown for three generations in ¹⁴N medium. What percentage of the DNA molecules will be light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N)?
questions.solution_md: After 3 generations there are $2^3 = 8$ molecules, of which 2 are hybrid. Light $= \dfrac{6}{8} \times 100 = 75$ percent.

questions.stem_md: Suppose DNA replication were conservative (the parent double helix stays intact and a wholly new helix is made). What would Meselson and Stahl have seen after one generation in ¹⁴N medium?

options.text_md: A heavy band and a light band, and no hybrid band
A hybrid band and a light band

questions.solution_md: Conservative replication keeps one fully heavy molecule and makes one fully light molecule, so two bands and no hybrid. The observed single hybrid band ruled it out — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Why is one new strand made discontinuously at a replication fork?

options.text_md: DNA ligase can join nucleotides only in the 3′ → 5′ direction.
Okazaki fragments are made by RNA polymerase.
DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 5′ → 3′ direction.

questions.solution_md: On the strand whose template runs the other way, synthesis must restart repeatedly, in short 5′ → 3′ pieces (Okazaki fragments) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand.
questions.solution_md: True. Okazaki fragments are later joined by DNA ligase.

questions.stem_md: At a replication fork, template strand X runs 3′ → 5′ in the direction in which the fork moves, and template strand Y runs 5′ → 3′ in that direction. Predict on which template the new strand is made continuously, explain why, and name the enzymes involved.

answer.model_answer_md: On **template X**. **DNA-dependent DNA polymerase** adds nucleotides only **5′ → 3′**, so each new strand is antiparallel to its template. On X the new strand grows 5′ → 3′ **towards the fork, continuously**: the **leading strand**. On Y the new strand must grow away from the fork, so it is made **discontinuously** as **Okazaki fragments**: the **lagging strand**. **DNA ligase** joins the fragments.

questions.solution_md: Apply the 5′ → 3′ rule to each template.

marking_scheme.step: Template X gives the continuous (leading) strand
Reason: polymerase works 5′ → 3′; lagging strand as Okazaki fragments on Y
DNA polymerase and DNA ligase named

questions.stem_md: A double-stranded DNA molecule replicates semi-conservatively three times in a row. Of all the DNA molecules formed, how many still contain a strand of the original molecule?
questions.solution_md: The two original strands are never broken up; each stays in one molecule. Of the $2^3 = 8$ molecules, the hybrid fraction is $\dfrac{2}{8}$, so $8 \times \dfrac{2}{8} = 2$ molecules contain an original strand.

questions.stem_md: Describe the experiment of Meselson and Stahl. What results did they obtain after one and two generations, and how did these prove that DNA replicates semi-conservatively?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Set-up.** E. coli was grown for many generations in a medium containing ¹⁵NH₄Cl as the only nitrogen source, so all its DNA became heavy. The cells were then transferred to a medium with normal ¹⁴NH₄Cl, and samples were taken after each generation (about 20 minutes).

**Separation.** DNA from each sample was centrifuged in a caesium chloride density gradient, where heavy, hybrid and light DNA settle at different levels.

**Results.** Before transfer there was one heavy band. After one generation there was a single band of intermediate (hybrid) density. After two generations there were two bands of equal size, hybrid and light.

**Interpretation.** If replication is semi-conservative, each daughter molecule keeps one old (¹⁵N) strand and gains one new (¹⁴N) strand, so all first-generation DNA is hybrid. In the second generation, the two old strands remain in two hybrid molecules while the new templates give light molecules, giving equal hybrid and light. Conservative replication would have given heavy and light bands after one generation. So DNA replicates semi-conservatively.

questions.solution_md: Set-up; CsCl; results; interpretation vs conservative model.

marking_scheme.step: Growth in ¹⁵N then transfer to ¹⁴N
Results after one and two generations

questions.stem_md: In eukaryotes, which RNA polymerase transcribes the precursor of mRNA (hnRNA)?
questions.solution_md: Pol I makes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); pol II makes hnRNA; pol III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In bacteria, the 23S rRNA of the ribosome acts as a ribozyme.

**Reason (R):** It catalyses the formation of peptide bonds during translation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the 23S rRNA is called a ribozyme because it catalyses peptide-bond formation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The coding strand of a gene reads 5′–ATGCCAGTA–3′. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
questions.solution_md: mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T: 5′–AUGCCAGUA–3′ — option (b). (a) is complementary to the coding strand.

questions.stem_md: Which polypeptide is coded by the mRNA 5′–AUG UUU GGC UAA–3′? (AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, UAA = stop)
questions.solution_md: Reading from AUG: Met, Phe, Gly; UAA is a stop codon, so no amino acid is added for it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a stop codon?
questions.solution_md: UGG codes for Trp (tryptophan); UAA, UAG and UGA are the three stop codons — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A single base is deleted near the start of the coding region of a gene. What is the most likely effect on the protein?

options.text_md: Every codon after the deletion is misread, so most amino acids after that point change.
Only one amino acid changes, and the rest of the protein is normal.
The protein is unchanged, because the code is degenerate.
One amino acid is removed, and the rest of the protein is normal.

questions.solution_md: The code is read contiguously in triplets; deleting one base shifts the reading frame, so all downstream codons change (frameshift) — option (a). Deleting three bases would remove one amino acid.

questions.stem_md: If the genetic code used two bases per codon (a doublet code), how many different codons would be possible with four kinds of bases?
questions.solution_md: $4^2 = 16$ codons — too few for 20 amino acids, which is why the code is a triplet ($4^3 = 64$).

questions.stem_md: A tRNA has the anticodon 3′–UAC–5′. Which mRNA codon does it pair with, and which amino acid does it carry?
questions.solution_md: The anticodon pairs antiparallel and complementary: 3′–UAC–5′ pairs with 5′–AUG–3′, which codes for methionine — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An mRNA has 75 nucleotides from the first base of its start codon to the last base of its stop codon. How many amino acids will the polypeptide contain?
questions.solution_md: $75 \div 3 = 25$ codons; the last is a stop codon with no amino acid, so $25 - 1 = 24$.

questions.stem_md: Because some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, the genetic code is said to be ______.
questions.solution_md: Degenerate.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In some viruses, genetic information flows from RNA to DNA; this is called reverse transcription.
questions.solution_md: True. Retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA by reverse transcription.

questions.stem_md: The template strand of a stretch of DNA reads 3′–TACGGATTC–5′. Write the coding strand and the mRNA, with their 5′ and 3′ ends.

answer.model_answer_md:
Coding strand: **5′–ATGCCTAAG–3′** (complementary to the template).

mRNA: **5′–AUGCCUAAG–3′** (same as the coding strand, with U for T).

questions.solution_md: Complement the template; replace T with U for the mRNA.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three steps by which the primary transcript (hnRNA) of a eukaryotic gene is processed into mature mRNA.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Splicing:** the **introns** (non-coding intervening sequences) are removed and the **exons** are joined in order.

2. **Capping:** an unusual nucleotide, **methyl guanosine triphosphate**, is added to the **5′ end**.

3. **Tailing:** **adenylate residues (200–300)** are added to the **3′ end** in a template-independent way (poly-A tail).

The processed mRNA is then transported out of the nucleus for translation.

questions.solution_md: Splicing, capping, tailing.

questions.stem_md: State and explain any three features of the genetic code.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Triplet:** each codon has three bases; 64 codons, of which 61 code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons.

2. **Degenerate:** some amino acids are coded by more than one codon.

3. **Unambiguous and nearly universal:** each codon codes for only one amino acid, and the same code is used from bacteria to humans, with a few exceptions. (Also: read contiguously without punctuation; AUG codes for methionine and acts as the start codon.)

questions.solution_md: Any three features with explanation.

questions.stem_md: Why is tRNA called an adapter molecule? Name the two key regions that make this possible.

answer.model_answer_md: tRNA links the **language of nucleic acids** (codons) with the **language of proteins** (amino acids). Its **anticodon loop** pairs with a codon on the mRNA, and its **amino acid acceptor end** carries the matching amino acid.

questions.solution_md: Anticodon and acceptor end connect codon to amino acid.

marking_scheme.step: Anticodon loop and amino acid acceptor end

questions.stem_md: Draw and label a transcription unit. Describe transcription in bacteria, and explain how the process and its products differ in eukaryotes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Transcription unit (diagram).** Promoter (upstream, where RNA polymerase binds), structural gene, terminator (downstream); the template strand runs 3′ → 5′ and the coding strand 5′ → 3′.

**In bacteria.** A single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcribes all RNAs. It binds the promoter with the help of the initiation factor σ, opens the DNA, and polymerises ribonucleotides 5′ → 3′ using one strand as template. At the terminator, the termination factor ρ helps release the RNA. Because there is no nuclear membrane and no processing, translation can begin while transcription is still going on.

**In eukaryotes.** Three RNA polymerases work in the nucleus: pol I makes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S), pol II makes hnRNA, the precursor of mRNA, and pol III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs. Genes are split into exons and introns. The hnRNA is processed: introns are removed by splicing, a methyl guanosine triphosphate cap is added at the 5′ end and a poly-A tail at the 3′ end. Only the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus for translation.

questions.solution_md: Labelled unit; bacterial process with σ and ρ; three polymerases; processing.

marking_scheme.step: Bacterial transcription with σ and ρ
Three eukaryotic RNA polymerases with products

questions.stem_md: Describe the process of translation in bacteria, including the role of tRNA and of the ribosome.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Charging.** Each amino acid is activated in the presence of ATP and linked to its specific tRNA (aminoacylation of tRNA).

**tRNA as adapter.** The tRNA’s anticodon pairs with a codon on the mRNA, and its acceptor end carries the amino acid; a special initiator tRNA carries methionine, and there is no tRNA for the stop codons.

**Initiation.** The small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA and finds the start codon AUG; the initiator tRNA pairs with it, and the large subunit joins.

**Elongation.** Charged tRNAs enter one by one according to the codons. The ribosome joins each new amino acid to the growing chain with a peptide bond; in bacteria the 23S rRNA catalyses this step, acting as a ribozyme. The ribosome moves along the mRNA codon by codon.

**Termination.** When a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) is reached, a release factor binds, and the polypeptide is released from the ribosome. Untranslated regions at both ends of the mRNA help translation to proceed efficiently.

questions.solution_md: Charging; adapter; initiation at AUG; elongation with ribozyme; termination.

marking_scheme.step: Initiation at AUG with ribosomal subunits
Termination by a release factor at a stop codon

options.text_md: The repressor, which binds RNA polymerase

questions.solution_md: Lactose acts as the inducer: it binds the repressor, which can then no longer bind the operator — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A mutant E. coli has a defective i gene and makes no functional repressor. How will its lac operon behave?

options.text_md: The structural genes are never transcribed.
The operon is switched on only when lactose is present.
The structural genes are transcribed all the time, with or without lactose.
Only the i gene is transcribed.

questions.solution_md: Without a functional repressor nothing blocks the operator, so RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a continuously — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the absence of lactose, what is bound to the operator of the lac operon?
questions.solution_md: The repressor made by the i gene binds the operator and prevents transcription — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The lac operon is an example of negative regulation.

**Reason (R):** The repressor protein of the lac operon is coded by the z gene.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the repressor switches the operon off. R is false: the repressor is coded by the regulatory i gene; z codes for β-galactosidase — option (c).

questions.stem_md: E. coli growing in a medium without lactose is transferred to a medium containing only lactose as its sugar. Explain the changes in its lac operon.

answer.model_answer_md: Before transfer, the **repressor** (from the i gene) is bound to the **operator**, so RNA polymerase cannot transcribe the operon; very little enzyme is made. After transfer, a few **permease** molecules let **lactose** in. Lactose acts as the **inducer**: it binds and **inactivates the repressor**, which leaves the operator. RNA polymerase now transcribes **z, y and a**, so **β-galactosidase** breaks lactose into glucose and galactose and **permease** brings in more lactose. When lactose runs out, the repressor binds again.

questions.solution_md: Off → inducer inactivates repressor → on → off again.

marking_scheme.step: Lactose inactivates repressor; transcription of z, y, a
Roles of the enzymes and switching off later

questions.stem_md: With a labelled diagram, explain the structure and working of the lac operon. Why is it called negative regulation?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Structure (diagram).** The lac operon of E. coli, described by Jacob and Monod, has a regulatory gene i, a promoter p, an operator o and three structural genes: z (β-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose), y (permease, which increases the cell’s permeability to lactose) and a (transacetylase).

**In the absence of lactose.** The i gene is transcribed and translated to make the repressor. The repressor binds the operator, so RNA polymerase cannot transcribe the structural genes; the operon is off.

**In the presence of lactose.** Lactose, the inducer, enters through permease and binds the repressor, changing its shape so that it cannot bind the operator. RNA polymerase then binds the promoter and transcribes z, y and a as one mRNA, and the three enzymes are made.

**Negative regulation.** The operon is controlled by a repressor that switches transcription off; the inducer works only by removing this block. When lactose is used up, the repressor binds the operator again.

questions.solution_md: Parts and products; off without lactose; on with inducer; why negative.

questions.stem_md: Why are VNTRs used as probes in DNA fingerprinting?

options.text_md: They code for proteins that differ between people.
They are identical in all humans.
They are found only in the Y chromosome.

questions.solution_md: VNTRs are non-coding satellite repeats whose copy number is highly polymorphic, giving each person a distinct pattern of fragment sizes — option (d).

It is RNA, because it contains four bases.
It is double-stranded RNA, because A is more than T.

**Reason (R):** A child inherits half its chromosomes from each parent.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by polymorphism in DNA, and why is it the basis of DNA fingerprinting?

answer.model_answer_md: **Polymorphism** is the occurrence of **variations in a DNA sequence** (such as different numbers of tandem repeats) between individuals of a population; it arises by mutation and is inherited. Since the pattern of such variable regions, like **VNTRs**, differs between people (except identical twins), comparing them can **identify individuals**.

questions.solution_md: Inherited sequence variation; unique patterns.

questions.stem_md: List, in order, the steps of DNA fingerprinting using VNTR probes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Isolation** of DNA from the sample.

2. **Digestion** of the DNA by restriction endonucleases.

3. **Separation** of the fragments by gel electrophoresis.

4. **Transfer (blotting)** of the separated fragments to a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane.

5. **Hybridisation** with a labelled VNTR probe.

6. **Detection** of the hybridised fragments by autoradiography, giving a pattern of bands.

questions.solution_md: Six steps in order.

questions.stem_md: A court is asked to accept a DNA fingerprint match between a crime-scene sample and a suspect as evidence. Explain the principle and steps of DNA fingerprinting, and evaluate how much weight such evidence should carry.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Principle.** A large part of human DNA consists of repeated sequences. Some, the VNTRs, vary in the number of repeats between individuals (polymorphism). Because each person inherits a particular combination from the parents, the sizes of these fragments form a pattern that is practically unique to each person, except identical twins.

**Steps.** DNA is isolated from the sample (blood, hair root, skin cells), cut with restriction endonucleases, the fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis, blotted onto a membrane, hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe and detected by autoradiography as a pattern of bands, which is compared between samples.

**Evaluation.** A full match at many VNTR loci makes it extremely unlikely that the sample came from someone else, so it is strong evidence that the suspect’s DNA was present at the scene. But it does not by itself prove guilt: DNA may have been left innocently, samples can be contaminated or mixed up, and identical twins share patterns. The evidence should be weighed with the other facts of the case and the care taken in collecting and testing samples.

questions.solution_md: Principle; steps; balanced evaluation.

A class repeated, on paper, a set of classic experiments with pneumococci and mice.

| Group | Injected into mice | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Live S strain | Mice died |
| 2 | Live R strain | Mice lived |
| 3 | Heat-killed S strain | Mice lived |
| 4 | Heat-killed S + live R | Mice died |
| 5 | Heat-killed S treated with protease + live R | Mice died |
| 6 | Heat-killed S treated with DNase + live R | Mice lived |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) Group 4

**(b)** 3

**(c)** (i) In group 5 the **proteins** of the dead S cells were destroyed, yet the R cells were still transformed and the mice died. In group 6 the **DNA** was destroyed and transformation **stopped**. So the transforming principle is **DNA**, not protein.

**OR** (ii) The mice would **die**. RNase destroys RNA but not DNA, and Avery’s group found that RNase **does not prevent transformation**; the intact **DNA** still transforms R cells into virulent S cells.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Neither heat-killed S nor live R alone kills mice; together they do, so something from dead S cells transformed R cells — option (d).

**(b)** The mice died in groups 1, 4 and 5, so the answer is 3.

**(c)** (i) Protease no effect; DNase blocks.

(ii) RNase leaves DNA intact.
